title: Ratio tables: scale by multiplying
observableEvidence: Extends a ratio table using a consistent scale factor to find a missing quantity.
explanation:
A ratio table lists equivalent ratios. Each row describes the same relationship.

Example: a soup recipe uses 3 carrots for every 2 potatoes.
Carrots: 3, 6, 9, 15
Potatoes: 2, 4, 6, 10
From 3 and 2 to 6 and 4, both numbers were multiplied by 2. From 3 and 2 to 15 and 10, both numbers were multiplied by 5.

The rule: multiply (or divide) both quantities in a row by the same number. Multiply both numbers, not just one of them. Adding the same amount to both does not keep the ratio: adding 4 to both 3 and 2 gives 7 carrots for 6 potatoes, which is fewer carrots for each potato.

When the factor is not a whole number, use a helpful row in between. To go from 6 carrots and 4 potatoes to 15 carrots, divide both numbers by 2 to get 3 and 2, then multiply both by 5 to get 15 and 10.

A unit row is often useful. Dividing 3 and 2 by 2 gives 1.5 carrots for 1 potato. Dividing 3 and 2 by 3 gives 1 carrot for 2/3 of a potato. Keep track of which quantity is "for one."

Comparing two ratios: scale both tables until one quantity is the same, then compare the other quantity. Recipe A uses 3 carrots for every 2 potatoes. Recipe B uses 4 carrots for every 3 potatoes. With 6 potatoes, Recipe A uses 9 carrots and Recipe B uses 8 carrots, so Recipe A has more carrots for each potato.
workedExample:
Team A scores 3 goals in every 4 games. Complete the table for 8, 12 and 20 games.
Games: 4, 8, 12, 20
Goals: 3, 6, 9, 15
8 games = 4 × 2, so goals = 3 × 2 = 6. 12 games = 4 × 3, so goals = 3 × 3 = 9. 20 games = 4 × 5, so goals = 3 × 5 = 15.
Team B scores 5 goals in every 8 games. At 8 games, Team A has 6 goals and Team B has 5 goals, so Team A scores at the higher rate.

accessibilityNotes: The tables are written as labelled text rows, not as an image. No color or position carries meaning.
accessibleAlternative: Read aloud or display: A ratio table lists equivalent ratios. For 3 carrots for every 2 potatoes, the rows are 3 and 2, 6 and 4, 9 and 6, 15 and 10. Multiply or divide both numbers by the same number; never add the same amount. Use an in-between row when the factor is not whole. To compare two ratios, make one quantity the same. Worked example: 3 goals in every 4 games gives 6, 9 and 15 goals for 8, 12 and 20 games, which beats 5 goals in 8 games.
